---

## 2. THE FIRST-PARTY MECHANISM STATEMENT — the most load-bearing text that exists

**S1, p.2, verbatim [K]:**

> "The model developed by Renaissance for Medallion makes predictions that are profitable **only slightly more often than not**. Moreover, the predicted price movements can be easily overwhelmed by external events. To compensate for these factors, the model generates a large number of recommendations, so that by virtue of the mathematical principle known as the law of large numbers, the variability of the returns produced by the model is greatly reduced."

> "However, because the model's recommendations are expected to be profitable only slightly more often than not, **the rate of return obtained by applying the recommendations to an unleveraged portfolio would be very small.** Leverage magnifies the effect of positive changes in the overall value of the portfolio on the rate of return…"

This is the entire primary basis for the "51% win rate" folklore. **It contains no number.** It is Grinold breadth stated by the firm in its own words, plus an explicit admission that the *unleveraged* return is "very small."

---

## 3. HARD PRIMARY NUMBERS (all [K], all from S2 unless noted)

**Holding period — the only real distribution in the public record.**
S2 PDF p.68 reproduces an excerpt of a chart *RenTec itself prepared*, "Holding Period Comparison RIEF vs. Medallion, From January 1, 2007 thru March 31, 2009," Bates `SEC_RT13_010650-651` [Sealed Exhibit]:

| Lots relieved in | MED | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|
| 3 months | 12.25% | **86.97%** |
| 4 mo | 5.95% | 92.91% |
| 5 mo | 2.92% | 95.84% |
| 6 mo | 1.57% | **97.41%** |
| 12 mo | 0.10% | 99.84% |
| over 1 year | 0.16% | 100.00% |

Report text: *"RenTec's Medallion funds held positions for less than three months 87% of the time. They held positions for over six months less than 1% of the time."*

⚠ **What this source cannot see:** the excerpt **starts at 3 months**. The 1- and 2-month buckets (≈74.7% of lots, by [I] subtraction: 86.97 − 12.25) are **not in the public record**. There is **no primary source for a Medallion holding period finer than "under 3 months"**. Anyone quoting "holding period of *x* days" for Medallion positions is not citing this table.

**Do not confuse with option tenor.** Two separate, real, and much-conflated numbers:
- S1 p.3 [K]: *"the average holding period of the Deutsche Bank options from 2000 to 2009 was **455 days**"* (first DB option, a 2000 test trade, excluded).
- S2 PDF p.67 [K]: a **May 2010 SEC examination report** found *"the average length of the 42 options RenTec had exercised to that point was **385 days**."*

Both are **basket-option contract tenors**, not position holding periods.

**Volume / breadth.** S2 PDF p.67 [K]: the same SEC exam found that from **1 Apr 2008 to 31 Mar 2009** RenTec placed *"approximately **129 million trade orders**, involving nearly **10,000 different financial instruments** across **18 countries**."* RenTec told PSI it "recommended" **100,000–150,000 trades per day at each of the two banks** (6/27/2014 letter, `PSI-Renaissance-37-000001-000007` at 004), which PSI converts to **26–39 million trades/year** through the option accounts (PDF p.54). Barclays internal memo (11/18/2008) described Medallion as *"very high frequency trading."*

**Leverage — actuals, quoted by PSI from RenTec's own IRS submission** (S2 PDF pp.84–85) [K]:
- Reg-T prime brokerage would cap RenTec at **2:1**; its JBO broker-dealer arrangement at **≈7.6:1**; the JBO fund's realized average **4.6:1** in 2005–06, peak **6.4:1**.
- DB offered up to **16:1**, later raised to **18:1**; Barclays up to **20:1**.
- **Realized: DB options averaged 11.7:1 (max 15.9:1); Barclays options averaged 12.9:1 (max 16.8:1), 2005–2006.**

The headline "20:1" is a **ceiling**, not a usage figure. Realized leverage was ~12x.

**Profits.** S2 PDF p.8 [K]: DB's MAPS options *"produced profits for that hedge fund totaling about **$17 billion**"*; Barclays' COLT options *"produced trading profits for RenTec totaling about **$18.5 billion**"*; 31 COLT options had peak total initial notional ≈**$62 billion**.
S2 PDF p.6 [K]: all basket options across all funds produced *"more than **$35 billion** in trading profits, of which at least **$34 billion** came from options exercised after more than one year."*
S3 press release [K]: *"basket options produced about **$34 billion** in trading profits for **RenTec alone**."*
⚠ **[I] The press release and the report body disagree** — the body's RenTec-specific per-bank figures sum to ≈$35.5bn while attributing $34bn to the *cross-fund* long-tenor subset. Cite the body, not the release.

**Taxes.** S3 [K]: *"tax avoidance from the use of these basket option structures **from 2000 to 2013** likely exceeded **$6 billion**"* — across **all** users. S2 PDF p.8 [K] gives only two audited slices: SEC found five MAPS funds incl. RenTec *"saved a total of $779 million in taxes"* Apr 2003–Oct 2007, and COLT deferred *"$140 million of taxes"* 2002–2007.
⚠ The ubiquitous **"$6.8 billion Renaissance saved, 2005–2015"** is **not in the PSI report** (I grepped: zero hits for "6.8 billion") and its date window matches no PSI window. It is a post-2021 press artifact drifted from the $6bn all-funds 2000–2013 figure. **[UNKNOWN] provenance.**

**Current structure (S4, snapshot as of the ADV report's own stamp 7/1/2026, fetched 2026-09-05) [K]:**
- Total RAUM **$96,378,537,116**, all discretionary, **14 accounts**, of which **$4,558,527,680** attributable to non-US persons.
- **MEDALLION HOLDINGS LLC** (805-4961509683, Delaware) is the **master fund**; feeders: MEDALLION ASSOCIATES L.P., MEDALLION FUND L.P., MEDALLION INTERNATIONAL LTD., MEDALLION USA L.P.
- **Current gross asset value of Medallion Holdings LLC: $61,177,067,368.** Beneficial owners: **549**. **80%** beneficially owned by RenTec and its related persons. **1%** non-US. Minimum investment commitment $25,000.
- ⚠ **[I]** "Gross asset value" on Form ADV Schedule D includes leverage and is not net equity. This number is **not comparable** to the "$10bn capacity cap" folklore, which refers to net capital. Do not put them in the same sentence.

---

## 4. RETURNS: DOCUMENTED vs INFERRED — and the fee wedge

**Fee structure — first-party [K].** Simons, TED2015 transcript:
> Chris Anderson: *"Five and 44. So five percent flat, 44 percent of upside."*
> Jim Simons: *"We charged the highest fees in the world at one time. Five and 44, that's what we charge."*

That is the **only first-party attestation of 5/44** I located. **[UNKNOWN]:** the year 5/44 took effect, whether it was ever different (the commonly-cited "5/36 before 2002" has no primary source I could find), and whether it is current — S4 Part 1A carries no fee schedule.

**The returns chain — this is the critical structural fact.**

> **Every published Medallion return figure descends from ONE journalistic table: Zuckerman (2019) Appendix 1.** Cornell (2020) states his data *"is reproduced as Table 1 here"* from that appendix. Guo & Liu (2024) state they take Medallion fund sizes and trading profits *"from Appendix 1 of Zuckerman (2019)."* There is no audited, filed, or regulator-verified Medallion return series in the public record. **[K]**

| Figure | Value | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| $100 → | **$398,723,873** (start 1988 → end 2018) | Cornell 2020 | [K] restatement of S6 |
| "compound return" | **63.3%** | Cornell 2020 | [K] — naïvely chained annual returns |
| naïve compounded | **63.2%** | Guo & Liu, recomputing from the same table | [K] — corroborates Cornell's arithmetic |
| Zuckerman's headline | **66.1% before fees / 39.1% after fees**, 31 yrs 1988–2018 | reported by Guo & Liu quoting S6 | [K]; Guo & Liu note 66.1% *"is probably the simple average of yearly net returns"* and they get 66.0% that way |
| **capital-weighted compounded, before fees** | **31.8%** | Guo & Liu (2024) | [K] — **the correction** |
| log return / vol / modified Sharpe | 27.60% / 19.65% / **1.40** | Guo & Liu | [K] |
| Sharpe | *"exceeding 2.0"* | Cornell 2020 | [K], on S6 data |
| Sharpe **7.5 (2004)** | — | **[UNKNOWN] — no primary source located.** Traced only to unsourced blog/Medium posts. | **UNSOURCED FOLKLORE** |

**Why the gap.** Guo & Liu, verbatim [K]: *"With a compounded return of 63.2%, 20 million, the fund size of Medallion at the beginning of 1988 … would become a staggering 78 trillion at the end of 2018. This is doubtlessly an absurd amount of money and wrong egregiously because the total trading profit of Medallion for 31 years up to 2018 is only a little bit over 100 billion."* Medallion's size was **discontinuous** — capped ≈$5.2bn 2002–2009 and ≈$10bn 2010–2018 — so profits were distributed out, not compounded. Their sub-period result [K]: **51.8% for the first 14 years, 19.1% for the last 17.**

**[I] Operative reading:** the famous ~66% is (a) *before* 5/44, (b) an arithmetic-mean-or-naïve-chain on a fund whose capital was force-held constant, and (c) dominated by a $20m starting base. Capital-weighted and gross of fees it is **31.8%**; the last 17 years at scale, **19.1%**.

---

## 6. LOAD-BEARING FOR THE ASKING SYSTEM

1. **The firm's own words say the unleveraged edge is "very small" and that leverage — realized ~12:1, ceiling 20:1, obtained through a structure the IRS ultimately extracted ~$7bn over — is what converts it into a business.** The asking system has a **negative** per-trade net (−$0.057). Grinold with a negative IC: breadth and leverage both scale the loss. Medallion is not a template for "add breadth"; it is the proof that breadth only works on a positive-after-cost per-decision edge.
2. **Medallion's documented per-decision skill is unmeasured, not measured-and-small.** The asking system has something Renaissance's public record does not: an actual out-of-fold Brier decomposition with a CI. Do not benchmark a measured −0.0025 skill score against an unsourced 0.015 IC — the latter is not a measurement.
3. **97% of positions closed inside 6 months, ≥129M orders/yr across ~10,000 instruments in 18 countries.** That is the breadth scale at which "slightly more often than not" was made to pay, after real costs — and it was still not enough without ~12x leverage.
4. **The Medallion return literature is a one-source graph.** Cornell and Guo & Liu are not independent confirmations of each other; both are analyses of Zuckerman's Appendix 1. Any downstream agent citing "Medallion returned 66%" is citing a journalist's table, not a filing.

## KILLED

**K1. §2 headline — "Medallion's equity positions were held for weeks to months, not seconds" / "the seconds-scale HFT picture is folklore." REFUTED by the same document, five times.** [K]
- `psi_report.txt:264-266` (printed p. 2): *"the investment advisor used algorithms to engage in a high volume of trading, executing more than 100,000 transactions per day. **Many of those trading positions lasted minutes, and the overall composition of the securities basket changed on a second-to-second basis.**"* (The algorithm + 100k/day pairing is uniquely RenTec — the report's own contrast at `:3545` says George Weiss *"did not trade as frequently nor did it rely on a trading algorithm."*) [K quote / I attribution]
- `:165`: *"most of which were short-term transactions and **some of which lasted only seconds**."*
- `:314`: *"even trades that had **lasted a few seconds** or were executed the day before the option was exercised…"*
- `:2104`: *"'The trade is done within milliseconds ….'"* (Barclays DMA, RenTec.)
- `:2595` (p. 51): Barclays internal memo described Medallion as *"very high frequency trader."* Repeated at fn 337, `:3145`: *"very high frequency trading."*

The agent's §2 cited the holding-period chart and never quoted any of these. **The report's headline characterisation of RenTec is the opposite of the agent's.**

**K2. §2's inference from the chart is unsound — the excerpt is truncated at its finest end.** [K]
`:3154`: *"An **excerpt** from that chart, reprinted below…"* The printed table begins at the *3 months* row with cumulative 86.97%. Everything faster than 3 months — 74.72% of lots — is a **single unresolved residual**, not a "weeks" bucket. "The table's finest bucket is *months*" is an artefact of the excerpt, not of the data. Separately, the unit is **"Lots Relieved In"** — tax lots in an IRS/long-vs-short-term-gain proceeding, top-coded at "over 1 year" because that is the only boundary the proceeding cared about. It cannot bound position lifetime downward at all.

**K3. §6.3 — "Medallion held equity positions ≥1 month ~75% of the time." Self-contradictory and inverted.** [K]
The agent's own §2 computed 86.97 − 12.25 = **74.72%** and labelled it *"≤2 months"*. In §6 the identical number is re-labelled **"≥1 month"**. Both cannot hold. Under the report's own convention (`:318-320`: *"97% of the assets held for less than 6 months"*; `:3155`: *"less than three months 87% of the time"*), 74.72% is the mass **below** 3 months — which includes seconds. Verified: `86.97-12.25 = 74.72`.

**K4. §6.3 — "The documented cost solution is horizon, not cleverness."** Falls with K1–K3; there is no primary support for a long horizon, and direct primary evidence against it. The recommendation built on it ("grow gross move per trade ~3.2× via a longer horizon") is **unsourced**. (The arithmetic `0.0825/0.0255 = 3.235` checks out; only the RenTec warrant is dead.)

### B-1. **KILLED — the "two routes agree" corroboration is an artifact of a 2× double-count. This is the report's central quantitative failure.**

PSI, verbatim (`psi_report.txt` off. 192814, repeated off. 234067): *"RenTec estimated that the company conducted from 100,000 to 150,000 trades per day **with each bank**.286 Those estimates of the daily trading activities at each bank yield a **combined estimated average of 26-39 million trades per year** through the option accounts.287"*

The research uses **both** halves of that sentence in the **same table**, and they are mutually inconsistent by a factor of **2.807**:
- Breadth cell: 200,000–300,000/day (i.e. it doubled "with each bank") → **373.3×–560.0×**
- Per-trade-profit cell: 26–39 M/yr. But 26–39 M/yr ÷ 365 = **71,233–106,849 trades/day**, not 200,000–300,000.

PSI's own combined annual number implies **133.0× – 199.5×**, not 373.3×–560.0×. (Even the most generous defensible reading — 200–300k/day but only on ~252 exchange trading days, compared to the bot's 24/7 calendar-day denominator — gives **257.8× – 386.6×**, still below the reported floor.)

**The consequence is worse than the error.** Route A counts **orders** (129 M/yr); route B counts **trades** (26–39 M/yr). 129 M ÷ (26–39 M) = **3.31–4.96 orders per trade** — a perfectly ordinary order-to-fill ratio. **The report's qualitative thesis survives, and survives on its strongest evidence — which is not any of the arithmetic.** The load-bearing artifact is the RenTec Senate statement's own paragraph, confirmed verbatim, that the model is "profitable only slightly more often than not" and that unleveraged returns "would be very small." **Everything in the derived-quantities table (§2) should be treated as refuted or amended.** Three of its seven rows are dead (route-B breadth, $/trade, fee revenue), two are amended floors/ceilings, and the one methodological standard the asking system already enforces on itself — effective n over nominal n — was not applied.
